draft.title: Curve sketching with calculus
card: Intercepts
Put x = 0 to find the y-intercept. Solve f(x) = 0 to find the x-intercepts.
Turning points

Solve f'(x) = 0 for the stationary points and find each y-value. Check the gradient either side to see if it is a maximum or a minimum. Mark any point of inflection, where the curve changes concavity.
Edges
Check what f(x) does for very large positive and negative x. For a polynomial, the term with the highest power decides this.
Example

f(x) = x³ − 3x² = x²(x − 3) cuts the axes at (0, 0) and (3, 0). f'(x) = 3x(x − 2) gives stationary points (0, 0), a maximum, and (2, −4), a minimum. There is an inflection at (1, −2). As x → ∞, f(x) → ∞, and as x → −∞, f(x) → −∞.
draft.remember: Plot the intercepts, turning points and inflections, then join them to match the edge behaviour.

a.q: What does the graph of y = x³ − 3x² do as x gets very large and negative?
a.why: For large x, the x³ term outweighs the −3x² term. A large negative number cubed is a large negative number, so y falls without bound. The graph does not level off, because a cubic has no horizontal limit.
a.clue: Which term is largest when x is huge? What sign does it have for negative x?

b.q: For f(x) = x³ − 12x, what are the coordinates of the maximum turning point?
b.why: f'(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 2 or x = −2. f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16. The gradient is positive at x = −3 and negative at x = 0, so (−2, 16) is a maximum. (2, −16) is tempting but is the minimum.
b.clue: Solve f'(x) = 0, then check the gradient either side of each x-value.

problems.detail: The 'Turning points' line says to check the gradient either side 'to see if it is a maximum or a minimum'. This leaves out the third outcome, a horizontal point of inflection (as for y = x³ at x = 0). Students may think every stationary point is a turning point.
The card glosses a point of inflection as 'where the curve changes concavity'. That definition belongs to point 4 (second derivative and concavity); this point should only mention it.

check.summary: The maths, both questions and both explanations are correct. The card implies every stationary point is a maximum or minimum, leaving out horizontal inflections, and it briefly defines a point of inflection, which belongs to point 4.

final.title: Curve sketching with calculus
card: Intercepts
Put \(x = 0\) to find the y-intercept. Solve \(f(x) = 0\) to find the x-intercepts.
Stationary points
Solve \(f'(x) = 0\) and find each y-value. The gradient either side shows whether each is a maximum, a minimum or a horizontal point of inflection. Also mark any other points of inflection.
Edges
Check what \(f(x)\) does for very large positive and negative \(x\). For a polynomial, the term with the highest power decides this.
Example

\(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} = x^{2}(x - 3)\) cuts the axes at \((0, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\). \(f'(x) = 3x(x - 2)\) gives stationary points \((0, 0)\), a maximum, and \((2, -4)\), a minimum. There is a point of inflection at \((1, -2)\). As \(x \to \infty\), \(f(x) \to \infty\), and as \(x \to -\infty\), \(f(x) \to -\infty\).

4.alt: The graph of \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2}\). It has a maximum turning point at \((0, 0)\), a minimum turning point at \((2, -4)\), a point of inflection at \((1, -2)\), and cuts the x-axis at \((0, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\). It falls without bound to the left and rises without bound to the right.

final.remember: Plot the intercepts, stationary points and inflections, then join them to match the edge behaviour.

a.q: What does the graph of \(y = x^{3} - 3x^{2}\) do as \(x\) gets very large and negative?
a.why: For large \(x\), the \(x^{3}\) term outweighs the \(-3x^{2}\) term. A large negative number cubed is a large negative number, so \(y\) falls without bound. The graph does not level off, because a cubic has no horizontal limit.
a.clue: Which term is largest when \(x\) is huge? What sign does it have for negative \(x\)?

b.q: For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 12x\), what are the coordinates of the maximum turning point?
b.why: \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 12 = 0\) gives \(x = 2\) or \(x = -2\). \(f(-2) = -8 + 24 = 16\). The gradient is positive at \(x = -3\) and negative at \(x = 0\), so \((-2, 16)\) is a maximum. \((2, -16)\) is tempting but is the minimum.
b.clue: Solve \(f'(x) = 0\), then check the gradient either side of each x-value.
